documents.title: Generative AI
documents.summary: Office of Online Learning web page defining generative AI, listing capabilities, limits, educational uses, privacy and detector concerns. It advises faculty to state their AI rules in the syllabus and to redesign assessment, and sets no AI rule itself.
documents.stance_why: The page sets no ban or permission; it says 'In your syllabus, inform students whether they are allowed to use Generative AI programs in your class', leaving the decision to each instructor.

units.why: A definition of generative AI that sets what the page covers: 'designed to create new and original content'. It is informational, so definition type P61 and informs.
units.anchor: Generative AI refers to a type of artificial intelligence technology that is designed to create

units.why: Warns that generated references are unreliable ('fabricated citations'); this is a fact about output accuracy, so P31 with informs.
units.anchor: the references often deviate from the generated content or consist of fabricated citations

units.why: States a limitation that the tool cannot answer about recent events. A fact about output reliability, nearest type P31 though it concerns coverage rather than verification.
units.anchor: Inability to provide timely responses or address inquiries pertaining to recent events.
units.fit_note: Concerns the tool's knowledge cutoff, not wrongness of output as such.

units.why: Says users 'should exercise caution and critical thinking' and verify with trusted sources; a duty to verify AI output, so P31, should.
units.anchor: Users should exercise caution and critical thinking when interpreting and relying on its output

units.why: Lists 'Concept clarification' as an educational use of generative AI; this is AI as a tool for understanding concepts, so P12. A listing rather than a rule, so may.
units.anchor: Concept clarification
units.policy: Concept clarification is listed as an educational use of generative AI.

units.why: Lists 'Writing support' as an educational use; permission for writing help is P91, stated only as a listed use.
units.anchor: Writing support
units.policy: Writing support is listed as an educational use of generative AI.

units.why: Lists 'Coding and programming assistance' as an educational use. No existing type covers a bare listed permission for coding help (P16 requires conditions, P13 is debugging only), so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: Coding and programming assistance
units.policy: Coding and programming assistance is listed as an educational use of generative AI.
units.uncovered_note: Lists coding and programming assistance as an educational use of generative AI, with no conditions.

units.why: Says AI tools 'may share personal information ... with third parties' and train on it; a privacy fact, P50, informs.
units.anchor: may share personal information collected from the user with third parties, including vendors

units.why: Tells faculty to 'Talk to your students about responsible use of the systems that does not include personal information'; protecting personal data, P50, should, addressed to instructors.
units.anchor: Talk to your students about responsible use of the systems that does not include personal

units.why: Tells faculty to 'encourage them to read the Terms of Agreement and the Privacy Policy' before signing up. Reading terms of use is closest to P52 (terms of use), though the purpose is privacy; P50 is already used for the sibling unit about personal information, so I choose P52 with a note.
units.anchor: encourage them to read the Terms of Agreement and the Privacy Policy prior to signing
units.fit_note: Reading terms is advised for privacy reasons, not copyright or ownership of output.

units.why: States that detectors 'have a high rate of false positives'; unreliability of detectors is P39.
units.anchor: many of the tools have a high rate of false positives

units.why: 'Care should be taken to avoid viewing them as complete solutions' warns against relying on detectors, P39, should-not.
units.anchor: Care should be taken to avoid viewing them as complete solutions.

units.why: The Office 'will not support or endorse any of the products currently available'; an office position on detectors, P39.
units.anchor: the Office of Online Learning will not support or endorse any of the products currently
units.fit_note: The office declines to endorse detectors rather than saying they cannot be used.

units.why: 'We will continue to monitor the available tools and will update the campus as changes occur' commits to ongoing review of detector tools; nearest P54 but about detectors.
units.anchor: We will continue to monitor the available tools and will update the campus as changes
units.fit_note: Commits to monitoring detection tools and informing campus, not revisiting a policy.

documents.title: Resolution: AI-Powered Tools (S-2023-10)
documents.summary: Faculty Senate resolution (S-2023-10) treating AI-powered tool use without explicit written faculty consent as academic misconduct under the CSCU Code of Conduct. Acceptable-use details are left to each instructor's syllabus.
documents.stance_why: It calls unsanctioned use 'without the explicit written consent of the teaching faculty' misconduct but says procedures 'fall within the purview of individual faculty members via their course syllabi', so it delegates, with a restrictive default.

units.why: Whereas clause quoting the CSCU Code: cheating includes 'use of sources beyond those authorized by the instructor'; it is the definition under which AI use is judged, P36, informs.
units.anchor: beyond those authorized by the instructor in writing papers, preparing reports,

units.why: 'Academic honesty and integrity represent guiding tenets of SCSU' grounds AI rules in the integrity culture, P95.
units.anchor: Academic honesty and integrity represent guiding tenets of SCSU;

units.why: 'AI-powered tools are capable of convincingly simulating human responses' is offered as a ground for concern; no type states this concern about AI's human-like output.
units.anchor: AI-powered tools are capable of convincingly simulating human responses;
units.uncovered_note: States as a rationale that AI tools convincingly simulate human responses.

units.why: The Senate 'supports the continuing work of developing formal policies and procedures' with named stakeholders; ongoing work shows the policy is provisional, P54, although it also names who is involved.
units.anchor: supports the continuing work of developing formal policies and procedures for SCSU
units.fit_note: Also names the bodies taking part in developing the formal policies.

units.why: Resolves that 'unsanctioned use of AI-powered tools ... without the explicit written consent of the teaching faculty' is not allowed, i.e. AI is off unless the instructor consents in writing; fallback/default rule, P06 (the misconduct classification is coded separately as P36).
units.anchor: without the explicit written consent of the teaching faculty,

units.why: Same resolution calls such use 'a violation of the BOR/CSCU Student Code of Conduct part D.1, and therefore a form of academic misconduct'; classification as misconduct, P36.
units.anchor: a violation of the BOR/CSCU Student Code of Conduct part D.1,

units.why: 'specific procedures surrounding the acceptable use of AI-powered tools ... fall within the purview of individual faculty members via their course syllabi' hands the decision to instructors, P04.
units.anchor: the purview of individual faculty members via their course syllabi

units.why: 'the Instructor may impose appropriate academic sanctions per the guidelines outlined in the Faculty Senate document' gives the instructor sanction power under a procedure, P81; no concrete penalty is named so not P37.

documents.title: Academic Honesty
documents.summary: One line in the CS department's plagiarism definition names generating course evaluation materials with AI-powered tools and submitting them as one's own. The rest is general plagiarism, sanction and appeal text with no AI-specific guidance.
documents.stance_why: The only AI wording is that 'Generating CEMS using AI-powered tools and submitting [them] as one's own work' is plagiarism; this bans one use and says nothing allowing others, so prohibit applies narrowly.

units.why: Lists 'Generating CEMS using AI-powered tools and submitting [them] as one's own work' as plagiarism. It is both a ban on AI-generated submissions (P19) and a classification as plagiarism (P36); I chose P36 because the item is a member of the definition 'Plagiarism includes...', so the must-not is expressed through that definition.
units.anchor: Generating CEMS using AI-powered tools and submitting thenas one's own work,
units.fit_note: Also directly bars having AI generate course evaluation materials that are submitted as one's own (P19).

units.why: 'Your work should be yours and yours alone' is a general ownership rule that covers AI-produced work; P29. It is not AI-specific.
units.anchor: Your work should be yours and yours alone.

units.why: 'please see the following restrictions or consult with your instructor before submission' tells unsure students to ask; general rule, P10 (not AI-specific).
units.anchor: consult with your instructor before submission.

units.why: 'A faculty can employ any computational software and/or manual inspection to conclude that one or more students have plagiarized' allows tools and inspection to identify plagiarism, P40; not specific to AI.
units.anchor: A faculty can employ any computational software and/or manual inspection

units.why: Instructors determine sanctions and may impose a reduced grade, F for the assignment or the course; concrete penalties, P37 (applies to plagiarism including AI-generated work).
units.anchor: A grade of F for the assignment in question;

units.why: 'A student accused of academic dishonesty has the right to appeal an instructor's allegations' gives students a right to respond, P64.
units.anchor: has the right to appeal an instructor’s allegations.

notes: Coder B. The CS Academic Honesty page is mostly general plagiarism text; units there not AI-specific (P29, P10, P40, P37, P64) are coded because they govern AI-generated plagiarism too. No course-layer documents (deferred).
